Explain closures in JavaScript - how doe: A closure is formed when a function retains a reference to its enclosing lexical scope even after that outer function has finished executing - JavaScript doesn't garbage-collect variables still referenced by an inner function, so the inner function keeps access to them. This is what enables patterns like a counter factory (`function makeCounter() { let count = 0; return () => ++count; }`) where each call to `makeCounter()` produces an independent counter, since each returned function closes over its own separate `count` variable from that specific invocation.
Explain the JavaScript event loop - how: The call stack executes synchronous code first, to completion. Once the stack is empty, the event loop drains the entire microtask queue (Promise callbacks, `queueMicrotask`) completely before processing even one item from the macrotask queue (setTimeout callbacks, I/O, UI events) - this priority ordering is exactly why `Promise.resolve().then(...)` scheduled alongside a `setTimeout(..., 0)` always runs first, even though both are 'asynchronous': microtasks are drained to empty before the loop ever picks up the next macrotask.
How does prototypal inheritance work in: Every JavaScript object has an internal link to a prototype object, and property/method lookups walk up this prototype chain until found (or reach `null`) - objects inherit directly from other objects, rather than from a class blueprint. Classical inheritance (Java, C#) defines a rigid class hierarchy at compile time; JavaScript's `class` syntax is syntactic sugar over the same underlying prototype mechanism, meaning you can still dynamically modify an object's prototype at runtime in ways a truly classical language wouldn't allow - the flexibility is real, but it also means prototype chain lookups have their own subtle performance and behavior implications worth understanding beneath the class syntax.
Explain how `this` binding works in Java: For a regular function, `this` is determined by how the function is called (call-site binding) - as a method (`obj.method()`, `this` is `obj`), as a plain function call (`this` is `undefined` in strict mode or the global object otherwise), or explicitly via `call`/`apply`/`bind`. An arrow function has no `this` of its own - it lexically inherits `this` from its enclosing scope at the point it was defined, which is exactly why arrow functions are commonly used for callbacks inside a method that need to preserve the outer method's `this` without needing `.bind(this)`.
Explain Promises and async/await - what: A Promise represents an eventual value from an asynchronous operation, in one of three states (pending, fulfilled, rejected). `await` pauses execution of the async function (without blocking the rest of the program) until the awaited Promise settles, then either returns its resolved value or throws its rejection as a catchable exception - it's syntactic sugar over `.then()`/`.catch()` chaining that makes asynchronous code read like synchronous code. An unhandled Promise rejection doesn't crash Node.js by default in older versions but does emit a warning (and in newer Node defaults, can terminate the process) - always wrap awaited calls in try/catch or attach a `.catch()` so rejections are explicitly handled rather than silently or fatally unhandled.
What is variable hoisting in JavaScript,: Hoisting means variable and function declarations are processed before code execution begins, so they're 'known' to the scope from the top, even though assignment happens later in the code. `var` declarations are hoisted and initialized to `undefined` immediately, so accessing a `var` before its declaration line just gives `undefined` rather than an error. `let`/`const` are also hoisted but remain in a 'temporal dead zone' - inaccessible - from the start of the scope until their actual declaration line executes, so accessing them before that line throws a ReferenceError rather than silently returning `undefined`, which catches a class of bugs `var` would hide.
What is the difference between `==` and: `===` (strict equality) compares value and type with no conversion - if types differ, it's simply false. `==` (loose equality) performs type coercion before comparing, following a set of rules that produce surprising results (`0 == '0'` is true, `'' == 0` is true, `null == undefined` is true but `null == 0` is false) - these coercion rules are inconsistent enough that most style guides mandate `===` by default, using `==` only in the one narrow, well-understood case of intentionally checking for both `null` and `undefined` at once.
What is debounce versus throttle, and gi: Debounce delays invoking a function until a specified time has passed since the *last* time it was triggered - resetting the timer on every new call - used for a search-as-you-type input where you only want to fire the API call once the user pauses typing, not on every keystroke. Throttle guarantees a function runs at most once per specified interval regardless of how many times it's triggered - used for a scroll or resize event handler where you want regular, capped updates (e.g. checking scroll position) without the browser being flooded with a handler call on every single pixel of movement.
What causes a memory leak in JavaScript,: A memory leak occurs when objects that are no longer needed remain reachable (referenced) and therefore never garbage collected. A common example: attaching an event listener to a DOM element that's later removed from the page, without also calling `removeEventListener` - if the listener's closure captures references to other objects, those objects (and the detached DOM node itself) stay alive in memory indefinitely since the listener reference keeps them reachable, even though the element is no longer visible or usable. Single-page applications are especially prone to this since components mount/unmount repeatedly without a full page reload to naturally clear accumulated references.
What is the difference between CommonJS: CommonJS modules are loaded synchronously and resolved at runtime (Node.js's original module system), while ES Modules are statically analyzable at parse time (imports/exports must be at the top level, not conditional) and support async loading natively, which enables tooling like tree-shaking that CommonJS's dynamic `require()` can't reliably support. Mixing them causes issues because a CommonJS module's `module.exports` doesn't map perfectly onto ESM's named/default export distinction (importing a CommonJS module from ESM sometimes needs `.default`, sometimes doesn't, depending on tooling/interop settings), which is a frequent, confusing source of bugs when a project or its dependencies mix both formats.
Explain destructuring and the spread/res: Destructuring extracts values from an array or object directly into named variables in one expression (`const { name, age } = user;` or `const [first, second] = list;`), avoiding repetitive manual property access. The spread operator (`...`) expands an iterable/object into individual elements (`[...arr1, ...arr2]` to merge arrays, `{...obj1, ...obj2}` to merge objects), while the rest operator (same `...` syntax, different context) collects remaining elements into a single variable (`const [first, ...rest] = list;`) - together these make common patterns like immutable state updates (`{...state, updatedField: newValue}`) far more concise than manual object copying.
When would you use array methods like `m: Prefer `map`/`filter`/`reduce` for readability and expressiveness when transforming/filtering/aggregating a collection - the method name itself documents intent (map = transform each element, filter = keep matching elements) far better than a generic for loop with manual logic inside. There is a small performance overhead from the function call per iteration and (for chained calls) multiple passes over the array versus one hand-optimized loop, which matters for extremely hot, performance-critical paths processing huge datasets repeatedly - but for the vast majority of application code, the readability benefit outweighs a performance difference that's rarely the actual bottleneck.
What are WeakMap and WeakSet in JavaScri: WeakMap and WeakSet hold 'weak' references to their key objects (WeakMap) or values (WeakSet) - meaning if the only remaining reference to an object is as a WeakMap key/WeakSet value, the garbage collector can still reclaim it, whereas a regular Map/Set would keep it alive indefinitely just by referencing it. This makes WeakMap ideal for associating metadata with an object (e.g. caching computed data keyed by a DOM node) without preventing that object from being garbage collected once it's otherwise no longer used - at the cost of WeakMap/WeakSet not being iterable, since the garbage collector could reclaim entries at any time, making a stable iteration order impossible to guarantee.
What are the main tradeoffs of adopting: TypeScript adds static type checking, catching a class of bugs (wrong argument types, typos in property names, null/undefined access) at compile time rather than runtime, plus significantly better IDE autocomplete and refactoring safety in a large codebase. The tradeoffs: an added build step (compilation to JavaScript), a learning curve for the type system (generics, utility types) for teams new to it, and the reality that types only exist at compile time - they don't provide runtime validation, so external input (API responses, user input) still needs actual runtime validation (a library like Zod) since TypeScript's type annotations alone won't catch a malformed API response at runtime.
